Section 1

Executive Summary

From January 2023 to March 2026 (39 months), the shop ran 36.5K work orders and inspected 545K pieces at final inspection. 32.9K pieces failed, a defect rate of 6.0%, and scrap and rework cost $640K a year, 2.06% of revenue. The two charts below show the trailing twelve months, April 2025 to March 2026. In those twelve months the defect rate was 6.3% and scrap and rework cost was $638K.

The shop's defect rate target is set at 4.5% of pieces at final inspection, based on an analysis of the competitive landscape and published industry benchmarks. At 6.0% today, reaching the target is worth about $163K a year in lower scrap and rework costs at current volume and defect mix.

Pieces Failed and Defect Rate by Month (Trailing Twelve Months)
Scrap and Rework Cost by Month (Trailing Twelve Months)

This report is intended to detail the drivers of the shop's defect rates and scrap costs. After cleaning and integrating five disconnected data sources (ERP, MES, QMS, Receiving, HR), we examined the combinations of operating conditions associated with elevated defect rates.

The shop is already aware that jobs with material sourced from Supplier C are associated with a 1.21× higher defect rate than other suppliers, and that high-complexity parts have a 1.40× higher defect rate than low-complexity parts. We considered these findings and explain their root causes throughout this report.

We found six conditions that account for a significant portion of the shop's elevated defect rates. These findings are detailed in Section 2: (1) brake jobs on lots 2% or more off nominal thickness run at 1.83× the bend-angle rate of lots under 2%; (2) the first run of a new or revised part runs at 2.15× later runs; (3) the first brake job after a gauge change runs at 1.78× the bend-angle rate of a job on the same gauge; (4) jobs with no first-piece inspection, resulting from schedule pressure and rush jobs, run at 2.00× jobs with one; (5) operators in their first 50 jobs on a machine type run at 1.95× operators past 300; and (6) gauge steel on lots 60 days or older runs at 1.39× fresh lots.

The cost savings associated with bringing each of these conditions to a normalized baseline target is presented in Section 2. As seen below, these conditions overlap across jobs, and so these savings aren't directly additive across conditions. Jobs that have two or more of these conditions present have defect rates above 10%, underscoring the importance of targeted actions to address these conditions.

Section 2

Findings

Lots that arrive off nominal thickness produce bend-angle defects
1.83×
bend-angle rate, lots 2% or more off nominal
$26K/yr
at the under-2% rate
  • On brake jobs run on lots that measured 2% or more off nominal thickness at receiving, the bend-angle defect rate is 6.4% against 3.5% on lots under 2%: 1.83× higher defect rate on 2,286 jobs. The rate rises with every band, to 9.0% on lots over 4% (2.79× the rate on lots under 1%).
  • The shop's own report shows this as a supplier problem: Supplier C runs at 1.21× the others on all jobs and 1.39× on brake jobs. Within the same deviation band Supplier C's bend-angle rate is level with the others' (3.5% against 3.2% under 1%, 3.5% against 4.0% at 1 to 2%, 5.1% against 5.3% at 2 to 4%). The issue is with the presence of significant (>4.0%) deviation found in Supplier C's lots, which have a 9.4% bend-angle defect rate.
  • The variation present in Supplier C's lots is higher than other suppliers: 64% of its measured lots are 2% or more off nominal, against 22% to 27% for the other three.
  • The effect concentrates on the brakes and in the Bend Angle code. Lasers and the punch show a smaller rise in dimensional defects; welding shows none.
  • Likely driver: bend allowance and springback are set for nominal thickness, so a sheet that is thicker or thinner than the program assumes comes off the brake at the wrong angle.

The first run of a new or revised part fails at twice the rate of later runs
2.15×
first run against later runs
$21K/yr
at the later-run rate
  • The first work order run on a new part number or a revised drawing has a defect rate of 12.5% against 5.8% on later runs: 2.15× higher defect rate, on 1,121 first runs. The second run is still elevated at 7.8% (1.35×); from the third run the rate is at its settled level.
  • First runs are 3.1% of jobs: 434 on a new part number and 687 on a revised drawing. The shop's program, tooling and setup for a new or revised drawing are proven on the first production lot instead of before it, and this explains the elevated defect rate presented here.
  • Part complexity is a separate effect. High-complexity parts run at 1.40× low-complexity parts on all jobs and 1.37× on later runs alone, and the first-run elevation is about the same size at every complexity level (2.10× on Low, 2.13× on Medium, 2.05× on High).
  • The added defects are dimensional: the Dimensional code takes a larger share of failed pieces on first runs than on later runs (38% against 27%), meaning the parts come off at the wrong size or with features out of position.

The first brake job after a gauge change carries elevated bend-angle defects
1.78×
bend-angle rate, after a gauge change
$45K/yr
at the same-gauge rate
  • A brake job that follows a job on a different material thickness has a bend-angle defect rate of 6.2% against 3.5% for a job that follows the same thickness: 1.78× higher defect rate on 3,918 jobs. On all defect codes the multiplier is 1.57×.
  • The elevation is confined to the first job after the change. The second job is back at 3.7% and the third and later at 3.4%.
  • 36% of brake jobs follow a gauge change, and both brakes show the same elevated rate.
  • Laser cutting jobs show no elevation after a change of thickness (1.02×).
  • Likely driver: a gauge change on a brake means a tooling change and a new back-gauge and angle setup, and the first job absorbs the setup error.

Lower first-piece inspection rates result from schedule pressure and rush jobs
2.00×
no first-piece record
$125K/yr
at the rate with a first-piece record
  • Jobs with no first-piece inspection record have a defect rate at final inspection of 9.8% against 4.9% for jobs with one: 2.00× higher defect rates on 8,667 jobs. This is the largest row in the financial impact table.
  • Rush jobs run at 1.21× higher defect rates than routine jobs, and the first-piece check is skipped on 47% of them against 21% of routine jobs. Rush jobs with a first-piece record run at the routine rate; the rush elevation is the skipped check.
  • Rush setups are short: the median rush setup is 0.65 of the part's standard, and where setup runs under 0.6 of standard the first-piece check is skipped on 50% of jobs.
  • Rush work is 12% of jobs over the period and 21% in March, April and October, and first-piece presence falls in the same months.
  • Likely driver: the first-piece check is the step that catches a setup error before the lot is run, and it is the step dropped when a job is expedited.

Defect rate falls with an operator's experience on the machine type
1.95×
under 50 jobs against over 300
$22K/yr
operators under 300 jobs, at the over-300 rate
  • Operators in their first 50 jobs on a machine type have a defect rate of 11.4% against 5.8% for operators with over 300: 1.95× higher defect rate. The rate falls with every band: 1.38× at 50 to 150 jobs and 1.29× at 150 to 300.
  • New hires and operators covering a second machine type sit on the same curve. 6 operators were hired in the period, and 15% of jobs are run by an operator covering a machine type other than their primary one.
  • Jobs by operators with under 300 jobs on the machine type are 7.5% of all jobs.
  • Likely driver: the first few hundred jobs on a machine type are where an operator learns its setups, and the record shows the same curve whether the operator is new to the shop or new to the machine.

Cold-rolled gauge steel held past 60 days fails more often; other materials do not
1.39×
gauge steel, lots 60 days and over
$25K/yr
at the under-60-day rate
  • On cold-rolled gauge steel (16, 14 and 12 ga), jobs run on lots received 60 days or more before have a defect rate of 8.3% against 6.0% on lots under 60 days: 1.39× higher defect rate on 3,780 jobs. It is 1.35× at 60 to 120 days and 1.83× past 120 days.
  • Plate, aluminum and stainless show no elevation on old lots (1.01×).
  • 19% of gauge-steel jobs run on lots 60 days or older.
  • The added defects are through surface contamination, which increases to 16% of failed pieces on lots over 120 days against 4% on fresh ones.
  • Likely driver: cold-rolled sheet stored for months picks up surface rust and oil residue, which shows under finish and as porosity in welds.

Section 3

Financial Impact

Each finding translates into scrap and rework cost that could be recovered by bringing the affected jobs to their comparison group's defect rate. The estimate scales the segment's recorded cost by the proportional reduction in its rate: savings = segment scrap cost × (current rate − target rate) ÷ current rate.

FindingJobsCurrent rateTarget Est. savings / yr

2 · First runs of new and revised parts1,12112.5%Later runs (5.8%)$21K

4 · Jobs with no first-piece record8,6679.8%Jobs with a first-piece record (4.9%)$125K
5 · Jobs by operators under 300 jobs on the machine type2,7418.5%Operators over 300 jobs (5.8%)$22K

Total before overlap$263K

Assumptions and caveats. Scrap and rework cost is the technician's estimate on each QMS event, attributed to the work order. The estimates assume cost per failed piece is constant within a segment and that the full gap to the comparison rate is addressable, so they are an upper bound. The segments overlap: 26% of scrap cost sits on jobs in two or more segments, so the rows are not additive and the total overstates what all six actions together would recover.

Section 4

Methodology

Data Sources ERP part master and work orders (part revision, rush flag, due date); MES machine register and job log (operator, start and end times, setup and run minutes, program or tool set); QMS final and first-piece inspections and scrap, rework and use-as-is events; Materials lot receipts with the thickness check at receiving; HR operator roster with hire date and machine types. The analysis covers January 2023 through March 2026: 36,492 work orders and 545,421 pieces inspected. The shop runs seven machines (two lasers, two press brakes, two welding stations and one punch press) on two shifts, in lots of 5 to 25 pieces. The pipeline cleans these record faults before anything is measured: part numbers keyed in five formats, lot ids in four, operator names in id fields, duplicate final inspections, reversed job clock entries, the lot not scanned on 15% of orders, and the ERP start entered late on about 30%.
Pipeline Each system's extract is staged, cleaned and typed in dbt on DuckDB, joined on the work order in an intermediate layer, and published as marts that this report and the dashboard read. Every model carries schema tests, and the build is reproducible from the raw files.
Definitions Defect rate is quantity failed over quantity inspected at final inspection, after duplicate inspection entries are removed, volume-weighted across a group. First-piece results are not part of it. A multiplier is a group's rate over its comparison group's rate, with a 95% interval and p-value from 2,000 bootstrap resamples. Intervals are from a bootstrap over jobs, since pieces within a job share a setup, lot and operator. Annual figures divide the total over the period by its length in years (days in the window over 365.25). Scrap cost is material plus rework labor from the scrap and rework events, attributed to the work order. Hours into the day is the job start minus the operator's first job start of the day in the job log, where a day begins after a break of eight hours or more. Lot age is the job start minus the lot's receipt date. A first run is the first work order on a new part number or a revised drawing.
Experience Is Partly Estimated An operator's experience on a machine type is the count of their jobs on it in the job log, plus the jobs they had run before the log begins. That prior experience is estimated from tenure: years between the HR hire date and the start of the job log, at the shop's measured rate of 480 jobs per operator-year on the primary machine type and a quarter of that on the secondary.
Known Data Limitations 15% of work orders have no lot scanned at job start, and a further 25% run on lots whose thickness was not measured at receiving, so 40% of jobs have no deviation figure and are outside finding 1; jobs with no scanned lot are also outside the supplier and lot-age comparisons. A missing first-piece record is treated as a check not done, although some checks may have been done and not recorded. The ERP start time is entered late on about 30% of orders, so job timing is taken from the MES job log. About 4% of job-log rows had the start and end clock entries reversed and were corrected.
